turn.text:
Kleinkünstler, "500 after a deploy" is a symptom, so we'll build the incident model before anyone touches the code. The word "every" already helps. If every request fails right after a deploy, the cause is probably in what the deploy changed, not in some rare data path. That's an inference from what you told me, not yet evidence.

## Incident model so far

| Field | State |
|---|---|
| Symptom | HTTP 500 from an Edge Function |
| Expected | 2xx for the same requests before the deploy |
| Scope | All requests (reported, not verified) |
| Timeline | Started with a deploy (the cause of the failure is not yet shown) |
| Environment | Hosted or local? CLI version? How was it deployed? Still open |

## What "500" can mean here

The docs say a 500 from an Edge Function means one of two things: an unhandled JavaScript error, or your own code deliberately returning a 500 [1]. Failed Edge Function requests also carry an `sb-error-code` response header that names the specific error [2]. That header is the cheapest discriminator we have.

| Rank | Hypothesis | Why it fits | What would falsify it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `BOOT_ERROR`: the function fails to start. The docs list syntax errors, import errors or missing dependencies, and invalid configuration as common causes [3]. | Every request fails, and a bad deploy is the usual trigger. | The header shows a different code, or the logs show handler code running. |
| 2 | `EDGE_FUNCTION_ERROR`: the function starts, then an unhandled error is thrown or a 5xx is returned on a path every request takes [4]. Examples: a missing secret, or a changed upstream call. | Also fits "every request". | The logs show a boot failure before any handler log line. |
| 3 | Your own code returns `status: 500`, for example after a failed third-party call [1]. | The docs name it as the second of the two cases. | Searching the code for `status: 500` finds nothing reachable. |
| 4 | A resource limit (`WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT` / `WORKER_LIMIT`) [5]. | Possible if the deploy added heavy imports. | The logs name no exceeded limit. I rank it last because a plain 500 isn't the signature I'd expect, but I haven't verified the exact status mapping this turn. |

## Next test

The test is read-only and changes nothing. Call one failing endpoint and capture the response headers:

```bash
curl -i "https://<project-ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/<function-name>" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-anon-or-user-JWT>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{}'
```

Expected output is the status line, a few headers, and possibly a short body. Redact the project ref and the token before pasting. Never paste a secret or service key.

Then open the function's logs in the dashboard and find the first error entry after the deploy time. A boot failure and a runtime exception look different there. A boot failure means no handler log lines appear at all.

Interpretation, once I see it: the `sb-error-code` value plus the first log line will separate hypotheses 1 and 2 from 3. I'm not declaring a root cause yet, and a redeploy or rollback would only be a mitigation, not an explanation.

What is the value of the `sb-error-code` header on a failing request? If the header is absent, say so, because that is also evidence.
